summary: This unit teaches you to prepare, run and follow up the meetings of the board of a Jamaican public body. You will learn to plan the board's year, set the agenda, prepare and send board papers on time, check the quorum, handle declarations of interest, support the chair, work out votes, write resolutions and minutes, manage decisions between meetings, keep confidential records, and make sure the board's decisions are carried out.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to **manage a board meeting** from the planning of the year to the follow-up of every decision. The board you will usually serve is the board of a **statutory body**: a public body set up by a law of Parliament to do a particular job, such as a development agency, a regulator, a training body or a hospital authority.

A board meeting is where the board **governs**: it sets direction, approves plans and budgets, oversees performance and risk, and holds management to account. A well-run meeting gives members the right information in good time, deals with the important business first, makes clear decisions that are properly recorded and then makes sure they are carried out. A badly run one wastes the members' time and can make the decisions invalid.

**Who it is for:** board secretaries, company or corporate secretaries, chief executives' assistants, senior administrators who support the board, and anyone who may be asked to chair or serve on a board or committee.

What this means in practice

Prepare an annual calendar, work out notice and paper dates, and brief the chair.
Prepare the agenda and the papers
Set a timed agenda, use a consent agenda, and make sure each paper has a summary and the decision sought.
Make sure the meeting is valid
Check the quorum and attendance, record declarations of interest, and keep to the board's rules.
Run the meeting
Support the chair in managing time, debate, management attendance, in-camera sessions and online members.
Record decisions correctly
Word resolutions, count votes by the rules, handle amendments and write accurate minutes.
Handle urgent business
Use written resolutions or an extraordinary meeting only where the rules allow.
Keep records and confidentiality
Store signed minutes, protect papers and deal with requests for information lawfully.
Follow up
Send out decisions, keep the action schedule and help the board review how well its meetings work.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with short date and quorum sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: preparing a full meeting pack for a made-up public body, then running and minuting a role-played board meeting that includes a declared interest and a vote.

blocks.note: Learn the exact terms in the Revision section (consent agenda, in camera, written resolution, executive summary and so on) and practise the sums for dates, quorum, votes and attendance.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Boards, rules and planning the year

blocks.p: A board acts only within the powers given to it by the **law that set up the body** (its Act), the body's own **rules or by-laws**, and the **standing orders** that say how its meetings are called, run and recorded. The board secretary must know these documents well, because they decide notice periods, the quorum, how voting works and whether meetings may be held online.

head: Document
What it gives you
rows: The Act or other governing law
The body's purpose, powers, the board's size and who appoints members
Standing orders (rules of procedure)
Notice, agenda, quorum, voting, minutes, committees, written resolutions
Government guidance for public bodies
Reporting dates, financial deadlines, corporate governance expectations
Board charter and code of conduct
Members' duties, conflicts of interest, confidentiality
Delegation of authority
What management may decide without coming to the board

blocks.p: The **annual board calendar** is the yearly schedule that lists each board meeting and the main business to be taken at it. Build it in this order:

flow: List what the board must do in the year under the law and guidance
List what the board should do (strategy, risk, CEO appraisal, policy reviews)
Note fixed deadlines (budget, audited statements, annual report)
Place each item at the meeting that suits its deadline
Spread the load so no meeting is overcrowded
Fix dates early and send the calendar to members and management

ul: **Corporate plan and budget**: before the financial year begins.
**Audited financial statements and annual report**: in time to meet the deadline for submission to the ministry and for tabling.
**Quarterly performance and financial reports**: at each regular meeting.
**Risk review**, **CEO appraisal** and **policy reviews**: at set meetings.
**Committee reports** (audit, finance, human resources): before the matters they cover are decided.

blocks.note: A calendar that links each meeting to its main business prevents the common failure: leaving a legal deadline until it is too late for the board to discuss it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: When
What the secretary does
rows: Months before
Circulate the calendar; update the register of interests
About 3 weeks before
Draft the agenda with the chair and CEO; ask management for papers
About 2 weeks before
Papers due from authors; check against the template
Notice / paper date (set by the rules)
Send notice, agenda and papers securely to all members
A few days before
Brief the chair; confirm attendance and apologies; check the quorum
Meeting day
Set up the room or link; record attendance; advise on procedure; take notes
Within days after
Send the action list to management; draft the minutes

blocks.h: Counting days for notice and papers

blocks.p: The rules fix how many days before the meeting the papers must be sent. Count **backwards** from the meeting date. **Example:** the papers must go out 7 days before a meeting on Wednesday 14 May. 14 - 7 = 7 May, a Wednesday: the papers go out by Wednesday 7 May. If the rule is 10 days, the date is 4 May, which is a Sunday. The secretary does not leave it to Sunday: she sends the papers by the working day before, Friday 2 May. Check whether the rules mean calendar days or working days.

blocks.note: Public bodies in Jamaica are expected to follow the corporate governance guidance set by government for boards. Refer to the body's own rules and the guidance your instructor gives you, and do not quote clause numbers.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The agenda is settled by the **chair**, working with the **CEO** and the **board secretary**. The secretary drafts it from the annual calendar, the action schedule from the last meeting and requests from members and committees. Members can ask for items, but the chair decides.

blocks.h: What belongs on the board agenda

blocks.p: The board deals with **governance** matters: strategy, plans, budgets, major contracts and policies, performance, risk, audit, appointments and decisions that the rules reserve to it. **Management matters**, for example a cleaning roster, routine office purchases or how an officer files applications, are for the CEO and staff. The secretary should advise the chair to leave them off.

ul: Opens with **apologies, declarations of interest, minutes of the last meeting and matters arising**.
Puts the **big decisions early**, when members are fresh.
Gives **each item a time** and a lead presenter, and marks it **for decision, discussion or noting**.
Uses a **consent agenda** for routine items.
Leaves time for an **in-camera session** and for 'any other business', which should be limited to genuinely urgent matters.

blocks.p: A **consent agenda** groups routine items, such as noting committee minutes and routine reports, and the board approves them **together without debate** with one resolution. A member may ask for an item to be discussed. When that happens, the item is **taken out of the consent agenda and discussed on its own**. It saves time for important debate.
Papers are how members learn what they must decide. Set a **standard template**:

head: Part
What it contains
rows: Cover details
Title, author, the executive responsible, meeting date, paper reference
Purpose
For decision, for discussion, or for noting
Executive summary
On one page: the issue, the options, the recommendation and the exact decision sought
Background and analysis
The facts, options, costs, risks and how it fits the plan
Recommended resolution
The exact words the board is asked to approve
Appendices
Detail for those who want it

blocks.p: The **executive summary** (the short section at the front stating the issue, the decision sought and the recommendation) is the part that most helps a member deal quickly with a long paper.

ul: The rules set the paper date. Set an **earlier internal deadline** for authors, so you have time to check and chase.
Check each paper against the template and the plan before it goes out.

**Late papers** are the chair's decision. A new, major paper handed out on the morning of the meeting, for example a large contract, should be **deferred** unless the matter is truly urgent and members can judge it fairly. Members cannot decide well on what they have not read.

blocks.p: Many boards use a **secure board portal** rather than ordinary email. It **controls who can see the papers**, records who has opened them, protects confidential information and keeps one set of records. Whatever the method, remind members not to forward papers or leave printed copies where others can see them.

A few days before, the secretary meets the chair to go through the agenda, the timings, the likely points of difficulty, any conflicts of interest and whether a quorum is likely. This briefing is one of the secretary's most useful tasks.

The **quorum** is the minimum number of members who must be present for the meeting to make valid decisions. The rules set it, often as **more than half** of the members. **Example:** a board of 9 with a quorum of 'more than half' needs 5 (half is 4.5, so more than half is 5). A board of 11 needs 6. A board of 10 needs 6 (half is 5, so more than half is 6).

head: Situation
What the chair does
rows: Too few members at the start time
Wait for the time the rules allow, then adjourn if there is still no quorum
Quorum lost during the meeting
Stop taking decisions; wait or adjourn, as the rules say
A member leaves for an interest, and the rules say she does not count
Check the quorum again for that item; if it is lost, defer the item

blocks.p: **Example.** A board of nine has a quorum of five. Five members are present. One declares an interest in item 6 and leaves; under the rules she does not count for that item. Only four remain, which is below five, so **item 6 cannot be decided**: it is deferred to a meeting with a quorum. Always count again.
**A second example.** The quorum is five. Seven members are present. Three declare an interest in one item and leave. Four members remain, which is fewer than five, so the item is inquorate.

blocks.note: Decisions taken without a quorum may be invalid. The secretary records who was present at the start and, for each item affected, who was present for that item.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Deal with them as a **standing item near the start**, and again when an affected item is reached.
The member declares the interest and, as the rules require, **withdraws** from the discussion and the vote.
Minutes record **the member's name, the interest, and when she left and returned**.
The secretary keeps the **register of interests** up to date and reminds members at the start of each year.

blocks.p: Attendance rate = **attendances ÷ possible attendances × 100**. Over 10 meetings, a board of 9 has 90 possible attendances. If 72 were recorded, the rate is 72 ÷ 90 = 80%. For one member: attending 5 of 8 meetings is 5 ÷ 8 × 100 = 62.5%. Boards watch attendance because a member who is often absent cannot do the job and the quorum is put at risk.

ul: **Senior managers** attend for their items, at the chair's invitation. They present and answer questions, but they **do not vote**.
**Observers**, such as a representative of the ministry, may attend only as the rules allow and with the chair's agreement. The secretary checks the rules and for which items they may stay.
**Visitors and advisers** (for example the auditor or a lawyer) attend for their item and leave when it ends.

blocks.p: Board papers and discussion are confidential until the board decides otherwise. Remind members at the start. After the meeting, the secretary **collects any printed confidential papers left on the table and files or shreds them securely**, as the body's policy says. Protect personal data, and follow the access to information rules for any request from outside.

The **chair** leads the meeting. The **secretary** advises on procedure, records attendance, decisions and actions and supports the chair; she does not take part in the debate unless asked. If the chair proposes something the rules do not allow, for example to approve an item that must first go to the audit committee, the secretary **politely advises the chair of the rule and the options** (for example, referring it to the committee or asking the board to suspend the rule, if the rules permit).

flow: Welcome; confirm the quorum
Apologies
Declarations of interest
Minutes of the last meeting; matters arising
Consent agenda
Main decision items
Committee, CEO and management reports
In-camera session (if any)
Any other business; date of next meeting

head: Problem
What the chair should do
rows: Early items overrun, leaving too little time for strategy
Move swiftly to the strategy item and agree how to handle what is left (extra time, shorter reports, a special meeting)
Members drift onto a matter that is not on the agenda
Bring the debate back to the item and offer to deal with the other matter properly later
One member dominates, another is silent
Invite the quiet members by name; limit repeat speeches
A new paper is tabled at the last minute
Defer unless truly urgent and members can judge it
Heated disagreement
Remind members of the question before the board; summarise the points; move to a decision

blocks.p: An **in-camera** session is a private part of the meeting held without management (and the public) present. It deals with matters such as the CEO's performance and pay, a complaint about a senior officer, a legal claim or the board's own effectiveness. The record is kept as a **separate, confidential minute with restricted access**, and only the decisions that can be shared are reported in the open minutes.
The **deputy chair** presides. If there is none, the members present choose a chair for that meeting, as the rules say.

Before holding a meeting by video link, confirm that the **rules allow it**, and that all members can **hear each other, take part and keep it confidential**. Check the link and the portal beforehand and agree what happens if someone drops out: the chair checks that the quorum is still met.

If the secretary wants an audio recording to help write the minutes, she follows the **board's policy**, tells the members, and keeps or deletes the file as the policy says. The minutes, not the recording, are the official record.

blocks.note: The secretary should never be the one to settle a dispute between members. She advises on what the rules say and records what the board decides.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Decisions: resolutions, voting and urgent business

blocks.p: A **resolution** is a formal decision of the board, recorded in the minutes. A good resolution is **precise**: it says what is approved, by whom, how much, for how long or by when. Compare:

head: Weak
Strong
rows: 'The board agreed to look at the Portmore lease.'
'Resolved: that the board approves the lease of the Portmore office at the rent and terms in Paper 6, for three years, and authorises the CEO to sign.'

blocks.p: Give each resolution a **reference number**, for example 2026/14, so it can be found, cited and tracked later.

flow: A member proposes the resolution
Another member seconds it, if the rules require
The chair opens the debate
A member may propose an amendment to the wording
The amendment is debated and voted on first
The chair puts the (amended) motion to the vote
The result is announced and recorded

head: Rule
Meaning
Worked example
rows: Majority of those present and voting
Votes for must exceed votes against; abstentions are not counted
8 present: 5 for, 2 against, 1 abstains. 5 is more than 2, so it passes
Absolute majority (of all members)
More than half of all members, whether they are present or not
Board of 10: needs 6 votes for
Two-thirds of all members
At least two-thirds of the full membership
Board of 12: 8 votes. Board of 9: 6. Board of 10: 6.67, so 7
Chair's casting vote
A second vote to break a tie, only if the rules give it
Tie at 4-4: the chair casts the deciding vote only if allowed

ul: A member can ask that her **vote against** be recorded. The secretary records it in the minutes, with her name.
Record votes **for, against and abstentions**, and the names where a vote is by roll call.
Check the quorum is still met at the time of the vote.

blocks.note: To work out two-thirds, multiply the number of members by 2, divide by 3, and round **up** to the next whole number if there is a remainder: you cannot have part of a vote.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Route
What it is
Use it when
Weakness
rows: Written resolution (circular resolution)
A paper sent to every member, which becomes a decision when the required members sign as the rules say
The matter is clear and simple, and members are likely to agree (for example, a change to a bank signatory)
No debate; one member can ask for it to go to a meeting
Extraordinary (special) meeting
A meeting called outside the calendar under the rules, with proper notice
The matter is urgent and needs debate (for example, a major problem after a hurricane)
Costs time, and a quorum must be found at short notice

ul: A written resolution is valid only if **every member receives the paper**, **signs as the rules require**, and it is **reported at the next meeting**.
An urgent decision that needs discussion should not go by written resolution. **Call the special meeting.**
Use a written resolution for a simple, agreed matter; keep the signed copies with the minutes.

blocks.p: **Minutes** are the official record of what the board decided and why. They are not a word-for-word report of the debate.

ul: The name of the body, the date, time and place of the meeting.
The names of members **present**, **apologies**, and others **in attendance** and for which items.
Confirmation that a **quorum** was present.
Every **declaration of interest**, and when members left and returned.

For each item: the **paper reference**, a brief summary of the main points and reasons, the **resolution** in its exact words, the **vote** (and any recorded dissent), and **actions** with the person responsible and the date.
The time the meeting closed and the date of the next meeting.

blocks.p: Recording the **paper reference** links the decision to the information the board relied on, which matters if the decision is later questioned.

ul: Follow the order and numbering of the agenda.
Be **brief, neutral and exact**. Record decisions and the key reasons, not who said what, unless a member asks for a view to be recorded.
Use plain past-tense sentences: 'The board approved ... ' not 'It was felt that ... '.
Draft them soon, while memories are fresh, and let the chair see the draft before it goes to members.

flow: Secretary drafts within days
Chair reviews the draft
Draft circulated with the next meeting's papers
Board confirms them as a correct record at the next meeting (with any corrections)
Chair signs the confirmed minutes
Signed copy filed in the minute book

blocks.p: Signed minutes and resolutions are kept in a **secure, controlled minute book** (a bound book or a controlled electronic records system). Keep the papers, notices, attendance sheets and the in-camera minutes under the same control, with access limited to those entitled to see them. Follow the body's records policy and the rules of the national archives for how long to keep them.

When a citizen or a journalist asks for board minutes or papers, the secretary does not simply refuse or hand them over. The request is dealt with **under the access to information rules, with any lawful exemptions** (for example for personal data or commercially sensitive material). Pass it to the officer responsible and follow the body's procedure.

sections.title: After the meeting and reviewing meetings

blocks.p: Straight after the meeting, send management a **list of decisions and actions**, with resolution numbers, owners and due dates, so work can begin before the minutes are confirmed. When the board approves something new, such as a new policy, the secretary sends the decision to management to act on, with any deadline.

head: Meeting
Action
Owner
Due
Status
Comment
rows: Present revised procurement plan
Director, Corporate Services
Next meeting
On track
Draft with the audit committee
Report on staff vacancies
HR Manager
Next meeting
Done
Circulated
Review the insurance cover
Finance Manager
Overdue
Late
Waiting for broker's quote

blocks.p: The secretary keeps **one schedule of actions**, updates it after each meeting and puts it on the **agenda of every meeting**, so the board can see which decisions have been done, are on track or are late. This is how the board knows whether its decisions are being carried out.

A committee, such as the audit committee, reports to the full board by a **short report of its work, findings and any recommendations for decision**. The board decides; the committee advises, unless the rules delegate a decision to it.

Ask for two minutes of **feedback** at the end of each meeting: Were the papers clear and on time? Did the meeting keep to time? Was there enough debate on the important items? The main benefit is that the board can improve its papers, time use and debate.

**When members complain that meetings run for five hours and papers come late,** gather evidence first: review the last six agendas, minutes and papers to see how long each item took, how much time went on routine reports, and when papers were sent. Ask members in a short confidential survey. Then act: introduce a consent agenda, set earlier paper deadlines, limit paper length, move reports to 'for noting', time each item and agree changes with the chair.

blocks.note: Public bodies are expected to review the board's performance each year. A short meeting-evaluation habit gives the board the evidence it needs.
blocks.label: Jamaica

terms: Statutory body
A public body set up by a law of Parliament.
Standing orders
The board's written rules on how its meetings are called, run and recorded.
Annual board calendar
The yearly schedule of board meetings and their main business.
Quorum
The minimum number of members who must be present for decisions to be valid.
Consent agenda
Routine items approved together without debate unless a member asks to discuss one.
Executive summary
The short front section of a board paper stating the issue, recommendation and decision sought.
Board portal
A secure online system for sending papers and keeping board records.
Declaration of interest
A member's statement of a personal, financial or other interest in an item.
Register of interests
The record, kept by the secretary, of members' interests.
In camera
A private part of a meeting held without management or the public.
Resolution
A formal decision of the board, recorded in the minutes.
Amendment
A proposed change to the wording of a resolution.
Written resolution
A decision made between meetings when members sign their agreement to a paper.
Extraordinary meeting
A meeting called outside the normal calendar to deal with urgent business.
Deputy chair
The member who presides when the chair is absent.
Minute book
The bound or electronic record that holds a board's signed minutes.
Schedule of actions
A list of decisions and actions, with owners, due dates and status.
Board secretary
The officer who manages papers, advises on procedure and keeps the minutes.

c1.title: Preparing the May meeting of a development agency
c1.text: Ms Kerry-Ann Powell is board secretary of the St Ann Parish Development Agency, a statutory body with an 11-member board. The rules say papers must be sent at least 10 days before the meeting, and the quorum is more than half of the members. The next meeting is on Wednesday 14 May. The CEO wants the board to approve a new set of office-supplies prices and also to note three routine committee minutes.

c2.title: A conflict at the Cultural Centre board
c2.text: The board of a cultural centre has 10 members, and its rules set the quorum at more than half of the members. Seven members attend the meeting. During declarations, Mr Orville Bailey and Ms Carla Simms declare that they are directors of a company that has bid for the centre's lighting contract, and the rules say a member with an interest leaves and does not count towards the quorum for that item. Later, a motion on the centre's budget needs a majority of all the members, not only of those present.

c3.title: Urgent decisions at a community foundation
c3.text: The eight-member board of the Hanover Community Development Foundation must change the bank signatories before the end of the month, and it must also decide urgently how to repair a flooded training room, a J$3,800,000 job. The rules allow written resolutions if every member signs. The chair, Mrs Joy Gordon, asks the secretary to use a written resolution for both. Seven members sign the paper on the bank signatories; the eighth, Mr Everton Reid, sends a message asking for a discussion first.

c4.title: Minutes of a vehicle purchase
c4.text: At a board meeting of a parish sports council, the board debates buying a van for J$4,200,000. Nine members are present. The vote is 6 for, 2 against and 1 abstention. Ms Beverley Lawrence, who voted against, asks that her vote be recorded. The meeting then goes in camera to discuss the director's appraisal. The secretary, Mr Delroy Wright, must write up the minutes.

c5.title: A meeting that runs out of time
c5.text: Mr Desmond Clarke chairs the board of a regional authority. The agenda gave 30 minutes to a major budget decision, but routine reports took the first two hours, and one member has now spoken for a long time about a dispute with a supplier that is not on the agenda. Another member, joining by video, has lost the connection. The board secretary is sitting next to the chair.

c6.title: Following up and reviewing
c6.text: The 11-member board of a training agency met 8 times last year, with 66 attendances recorded in total. Its schedule of actions lists 12 actions from the year's meetings, of which 9 are complete. Printed copies of the confidential minutes for one meeting were found on the boardroom table the next morning.

questions.q: What is the quorum for the St Ann board, and by what date must the papers go out?
o: Six members; papers out by Friday 2 May, as 4 May is a Sunday
Five members, and Wednesday 7 May, which is seven days before the meeting
Six members, and Thursday 8 May, which is six days before the meeting
Eleven members, and Friday 2 May, because every member must be present
questions.why: More than half of 11 is 6. Ten days before 14 May is 4 May, a Sunday, so the secretary makes sure the papers go out on the last working day before: Friday 2 May.

questions.q: Which item is least suitable for the board agenda?
o: The review of the agency's three-year corporate plan and budget
Approval of the annual report and audited financial statements
The appointment of the chair of a new committee on audit and risk
Approval of the price of office stationery, a management matter
questions.why: The board deals with governance. Everyday purchases and prices are for the CEO and staff within the authority the board has delegated. Putting them on the agenda wastes time.

questions.q: How should the secretary handle the three routine committee minutes the CEO wants the board to note?
o: Give each one a full 30 minutes of debate so that no member feels left out
Leave them off the agenda and send them to members by email afterwards
Group them in a consent agenda, approved together unless queried
Add them to the 'any other business' item at the end of the meeting
questions.why: A consent agenda handles routine items quickly and still lets any member ask for one to be taken out and discussed on its own.

questions.q: With seven present, how many members count towards the quorum for the lighting-contract item, and what must happen?
o: Seven, because members with an interest still count as present
Five, which is below the quorum of six, so the item is deferred
Six, so the item can be decided if the two members vote against
Five, which is above the quorum, so the item goes ahead
questions.why: The quorum is 6 (more than half of 10). Seven present minus the two who left leaves five. That is fewer than six, so the board cannot decide the item and it is deferred.

questions.q: The budget motion needs a majority of all 10 members. Five vote for, three vote against and two members are absent. What is the result?
o: It passes, because five votes for is more than the three votes against
It fails, because it needs at least 6 votes in favour out of all 10 members
It passes, because exactly half of all members voted in favour of it
It fails, because three members voted against and so the motion is opposed
questions.why: A majority of all members means more than half of the whole board: 6 of 10. Five votes for is not enough, even though it beats the three votes against.

questions.q: What should the minutes record about the interests of Mr Bailey and Ms Simms?
o: Their names, the interest, and when each left and returned
Only that two members were absent from part of the meeting
The company's bid, so that all members can compare it with others
Nothing, because the interest is private business
questions.why: The minutes must show the declaration, the withdrawal and the return. This protects the members and the board if the decision is questioned later.

questions.q: Is the written resolution on the bank signatories valid, and what should happen next?
o: Yes, because seven of the eight members signed and that is a majority
Yes, as long as the chair signs as the eighth member to complete it
No, but Mr Reid's message can be counted as his signature
No: all members must sign, so the matter goes to a meeting
questions.why: The rules in this case say all members must sign. One member asked for discussion, so the written route has failed and the matter must be put to a meeting.

questions.q: What is the best way to decide on the J$3,800,000 flood repair, which needs debate and a firm decision this week?
o: Send a second written resolution and count the seven who sign
Let the chair decide alone and report it at the next regular meeting
Call an extraordinary meeting under the rules, with proper notice
Ask the CEO to start the work and seek approval after it ends
questions.why: An urgent matter that needs debate belongs at a special meeting, called under the rules. A written resolution gives no chance to question management.

questions.q: For which matter is a written resolution best suited?
o: A contract on which members hold sharply different views
A complaint about the CEO that needs a private discussion
A simple matter members agree on, such as a signatory change
A change in the body's strategy that needs wide debate
questions.why: A written resolution suits a straightforward matter on which members are likely to agree. It does not allow debate.

questions.q: What must happen to a decision made by written resolution?
o: It stays confidential and is never mentioned in the minutes
It must be reported at the next meeting and the signed copies kept with the minutes
It must be confirmed by a vote of all members at the next meeting before it takes effect
It lapses if the chair does not sign it within one working day
questions.why: The board must be able to see and record all decisions. Reporting it at the next meeting and filing the signed papers keeps the record complete.

questions.q: What was the result of the vote, and how should it be recorded in the minutes?
o: It passed 6 to 2, and her vote against is recorded by name
It failed, because 3 members did not vote for the motion
It passed 6 to 3, because the abstention counts as a vote against
It passed, but only the number 6 for need be recorded
questions.why: The rule is a majority of those present and voting: 6 is greater than 2. The abstention is not counted as a vote against. The minutes record the numbers and her request.

questions.q: Which wording is the best for the resolution on the van?
o: Resolved: that the council agrees in principle to a vehicle purchase for its work.
Resolved: that the council notes the proposal to buy a van and thanks the staff for it.
Resolved: that the CEO is authorised to buy transport as she judges best for the council.
Resolved: that the council buys one van at a cost not above J$4,200,000, as in Paper 4.
questions.why: A good resolution is exact about what is approved, the limit and the paper it relies on, so that no one can doubt what was decided.

questions.q: How should the in-camera discussion on the director's appraisal be minuted?
o: In the open minutes, with all the details given to every member
Not at all, so that nothing can ever be leaked
In the open minutes, but without a date or an attendance list
As a separate confidential minute with restricted access
questions.why: An in-camera record is kept apart from the open minutes, with restricted access. The open minutes only note that an in-camera session was held and any decision that can be shared.

questions.q: Routine reports have used up the time, and the budget decision now has little left. What should Mr Clarke do?
o: Cancel the budget item and put it on the agenda of next year's calendar
Let the reports continue, since members have already prepared for them
Move to the budget item at once and agree how to deal with what is left
End the meeting, since the agenda cannot be completed
questions.why: The major decision must not be squeezed out. The chair moves on and agrees what to do with the rest, such as a shorter later item or a special meeting.

questions.q: A member is talking at length about a supplier dispute that is not on the agenda. What is the best action?
o: Allow the discussion, since a supplier dispute may be important to the board
Return to the agenda item and offer to deal with it later
Ask the secretary to stop recording while the member finishes
Close the debate and move straight to the vote on the budget
questions.why: The chair keeps the meeting on its business, while recognising that the matter may be serious by offering to have it handled properly at a suitable time.

questions.q: The member on video has lost the connection. What should the chair and secretary check first?
o: Whether the quorum still holds and the member can take part
Whether the member's vote can be counted by a message sent later
Whether the meeting should continue as if the member had left on purpose
Whether the secretary may record the missed items for the member to listen to later
questions.why: Online participation must let members hear and take part. When a link fails, the chair checks that the quorum is still present and pauses if the member needs to hear a matter.

questions.q: What was the board's attendance rate for the year?
questions.why: 11 members × 8 meetings = 88 possible attendances. 66 ÷ 88 × 100 = 75%.

questions.q: What percentage of the schedule of actions is complete, and how should the secretary use the schedule?
o: 75%, and she keeps it to herself to report only at the end of the year
9%, because 9 of the 12 actions are not yet shown as done
25%, which is the share of actions that are finished
75%, and it goes on every agenda so the board sees what is late
questions.why: 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75%. The schedule is a board tool: it goes on every agenda so that late actions are noticed and chased.

questions.q: A citizen writes to a public body asking for copies of the board's minutes for the past year. What should the secretary do?
o: Refuse it, because board papers of a public body are always confidential
Send all the minutes at once, including the in-camera record, as public money is involved
Handle it under the access to information rules, releasing what the law allows
Ask the chair to decide privately and not record that the request was made
questions.why: Requests from the public are dealt with under the access to information rules, which allow release but also protect certain material, for example personal data and matters decided in camera.

questions.q: A paper on the agenda is marked 'for noting'. What does this tell members?
o: They must vote on it, but only after a long debate
They receive the information, and no decision is asked of them on it
They may amend it, but the secretary will not record the changes
They must keep it confidential, as it is not for discussion
questions.why: The cover of each paper says whether it is for decision, for discussion or for noting. A paper for noting gives information; members may ask questions, but nothing is put to the vote.
